Real racehorses.Seabiscuit: A small, unlikely champion of the Depression era, Seabiscuit beat the mighty War Admiral in 1938 and became a national hero.
Real racehorses.Red Rum: Red Rum won the Grand National three times, in 1973, 1974 and 1977, and was second twice, a feat unequalled at Aintree.
Real racehorses.Phar Lap: This New Zealand-born Australian champion won the 1930 Melbourne Cup. He died suddenly in 1932, and his heart is preserved in Canberra.
Real racehorses.Frankel: Frankel was unbeaten in 14 races from 2010 to 2012 and was rated the highest in the history of the official ratings.
Real racehorses.American Pharoah: In 2015 American Pharoah ended a 37-year wait for a Triple Crown winner. His name was misspelled in an online contest, and stuck.
Real racehorses.Man o' War: Man o' War lost only once in his 21 races, in 1919, to a horse named Upset. He is among the greatest horses of the 20th century.
Real racehorses.Winx: Winx, an Australian mare, won 33 races in a row from 2015 to 2019, including four Cox Plates.
Real racehorses.War Admiral: War Admiral won the 1937 Triple Crown, and was the son of Man o' War. He was beaten by Seabiscuit in a famous match.
Real racehorses.Arkle: Irish steeplechaser Arkle won three Cheltenham Gold Cups in a row, from 1964 to 1966. A Cheltenham ride is named for him.
Real racehorses.Black Caviar: This Australian sprinter won all 25 of her races, and she was famed for a huge stride.
Real racehorses.Desert Orchid: Desert Orchid, a gray steeplechaser called Dessie, won the 1989 Cheltenham Gold Cup, and was loved by British fans in the 1980s.
Real racehorses.Mister Ed: Mister Ed was the talking horse of a 1960s TV sitcom, and he's fictional, played by a palomino named Bamboo Harvester.
Real racehorses.Black Beauty: Black Beauty is the title horse in Anna Sewell's 1877 novel, written to promote kindness to horses. He's fictional.
Real racehorses.Shadowfax: Shadowfax is Gandalf's horse in The Lord of the Rings, lord of all horses. He's from Tolkien, not the track.
Real racehorses.Trigger: Trigger was Roy Rogers' palomino, a movie horse and not a racer, but his fame was huge.
Real racehorses.Silver: Silver was the Lone Ranger's white stallion. A fictional western horse, not a racehorse.
Real racehorses.Pegasus: Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek myth, sprang from Medusa's blood. He's a legend, not a racehorse.
Real racehorses.Spirit: Spirit is the star of an animated film, a mustang with no race record.
Real racehorses.Joey: Joey is the war horse in Michael Morpurgo's novel War Horse, which became a play and a film. Fiction.
Real racehorses.Maximus: Maximus is the Disney horse in Tangled, with a nose for sniffing out trouble. He's animated.
Real racehorses.Bullseye: Bullseye is Woody's horse in Toy Story 2 and not a real racehorse.
Real racehorses.Boxer: Boxer is the loyal workhorse in Orwell's Animal Farm, with the motto 'I will work harder'. Fictional.
Real racehorses.Epona: Epona is Link's horse in Zelda, named for a Celtic horse goddess. She's from a game, not a racetrack.

Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Ones: Scores only the dice showing one, so it's the weakest upper box. Reaching 63 points in the upper section earns a 35-point bonus.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Twos: Scores only the twos you rolled, and to reach the 63-point bonus, three of each number is the benchmark.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Threes: Counts only the threes, so a roll of three of them gives nine points, and it's the pivot of upper-section planning.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Fours: Scores the sum of fours, and getting three of them keeps you on track for the upper bonus.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Fives: Scores the sum of fives, and it's worth more than the lower numbers but less than the sixes.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Sixes: The highest upper box, up to 30 points for five sixes, and the best place to put a lucky roll.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Three of a kind: Scores the total of all five dice, and it's a lower-section box that rewards big numbers.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Four of a kind: Scores the total of all five dice, and it's harder to fill than three of a kind.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Full house: Three of one number and two of another score a flat 25 points, a name borrowed from poker.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Small straight: Four dice in sequence, like 1-2-3-4, scores a flat 30, and it's easier to get than a large straight.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Large straight: Five in sequence scores a flat 40, and only two combinations, 1-5 and 2-6, qualify.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Yahtzee: Five of a kind in one roll scores 50 points, and the odds of rolling one in a single turn are about 4.6 percent.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Chance: A wildcard box that takes the sum of any dice, and it's the place to dump a bad roll.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Royal flush: This is a poker hand, the best possible, a 10-to-ace in one suit, and Yahtzee has no cards.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Flush: Five cards of one suit is a poker hand, and dice have no suits.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Two pair: A poker hand, though in Yahtzee, rolling two pairs gets you no box of its own, which surprises new players.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Straight flush: A poker hand that needs suits, and dice have none.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Pair: A poker hand of two matching cards, and Yahtzee has no box for a lone pair.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.High card: The weakest poker hand, and Yahtzee's scoring has no such box.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Bingo: A game of numbered balls and called numbers, and not a Yahtzee box.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Snake eyes: Two dice both showing one, a craps term, and Yahtzee uses five dice, where it has no named box.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Boxcars: Two sixes on a pair of dice, a craps term, and not a Yahtzee scoring box.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Sevens: A standard die has no seven, so Yahtzee has no such box, though seven is the most common total on two dice.
Yahtzee scorecard boxes.Jackpot: A big prize in gambling and slot machines, and not a scoring box in Yahtzee.

From Norse mythology.Asgard: Realm of the Aesir gods, home to Odin and Thor. It was joined to Midgard by the rainbow bridge Bifrost.
From Norse mythology.Midgard: The world of humans, ringed by the sea serpent Jormungandr. J. R. R. Tolkien's "Middle-earth" is a descendant of the word.
From Norse mythology.Valhalla: Odin's great hall, where warriors slain in battle feast and fight each day until Ragnarok. Its name means "hall of the slain."
From Norse mythology.Bifrost: The burning rainbow bridge between Midgard and Asgard, guarded by the god Heimdall.
From Norse mythology.Yggdrasil: The enormous ash tree holding the nine worlds together. A dragon gnaws at its roots while a squirrel carries insults up and down it.
From Norse mythology.Mjolnir: Thor's hammer, forged by dwarves, always returning to his hand. Its handle was too short because of Loki's meddling.
From Norse mythology.Ragnarok: The prophesied end of the world, when gods and giants fight and the world is destroyed, then reborn. Odin is swallowed by Fenrir.
From Norse mythology.Valkyrie: Female spirits who choose which warriors die in battle and carry them to Valhalla. Wagner's operas made them famous.
From Norse mythology.Jotunheim: The land of the giants, home of Odin's old enemies. Thor visited it to fight and to feast.
From Norse mythology.Niflheim: A realm of ice and mist, one of the oldest, where the dishonored dead end up. Its name means "mist home."
From Norse mythology.Sleipnir: Odin's eight-legged horse, born when Loki turned into a mare. It could carry him across sea and sky.
From Norse mythology.Fenrir: A huge wolf, son of Loki, bound by the gods using a magic ribbon. Tyr lost his hand in the trick.
From Norse mythology.Olympus: A trap: Greek gods lived on this mountain, which is a real peak and the tallest in Greece. Not Norse.
From Norse mythology.Elysium: The Greek paradise for heroes, also called the Elysian Fields. It is a Greek afterlife.
From Norse mythology.Tartarus: The deepest pit of the Greek underworld, where Titans were imprisoned. Greek, not Norse.
From Norse mythology.Atlantis: A lost island city first described by Plato as a cautionary tale. Greek in origin, and likely invented.
From Norse mythology.Avalon: The mystical island where Arthur was taken to heal, and where Excalibur was forged in some tales. Celtic and Arthurian.
From Norse mythology.Camelot: King Arthur's castle and court, which was never a real documented place. It first appears in 12th-century French romances.
From Norse mythology.Excalibur: King Arthur's sword, sometimes drawn from a stone and sometimes given by the Lady of the Lake. British legend.
From Norse mythology.Pegasus: The winged horse of Greek myth, sprung from Medusa's blood. Also the name of a constellation.
From Norse mythology.River Styx: The Greek underworld river that the dead crossed with Charon. Oaths sworn on it were binding even to gods.
From Norse mythology.Aegis: A protective shield or cloak of Zeus and Athena. We still say "under the aegis of" to mean under protection.
From Norse mythology.Trident: The three-pronged spear of Poseidon, the Greek sea god. Neptune carried it too, but the Norse gods did not.
From Norse mythology.Hydra: A Greek serpent with many heads, killed by Heracles. Norse monsters are different, like Jormungandr.

Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Hades: Greek god of the dead, who ruled the underworld that shares his name. He rarely left it, and wore a helmet of invisibility.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Pluto: The Roman name for Hades, and the name later given to the dwarf planet found in 1930. An 11-year-old girl suggested it.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Osiris: Egyptian god of the dead and rebirth, murdered and dismembered by his brother Set, then reassembled by Isis.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Anubis: The jackal-headed Egyptian god who guided souls and presided over mummification. He weighed hearts against a feather.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Hel: Norse goddess who ruled the realm of the same name, home to those who died of illness or age. The English word "hell" is related.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Persephone: Queen of the Greek underworld, forced to spend part of each year there after eating pomegranate seeds. Her return brings spring.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Yama: The Hindu and Buddhist god of death, said to be the first mortal to die. He judges the dead.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Mictlantecuhtli: Aztec lord of Mictlan, the land of the dead. He's shown as a skeleton wearing a necklace of eyeballs.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Ereshkigal: Mesopotamian queen of the underworld, sister of Inanna. One tale has Inanna descend to the underworld, and the queen kills her.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Dis Pater: A Roman god of the underworld and wealth, whose name means "rich father" and is equal to Pluto. Caesar claimed Gauls descended from him.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Orcus: A Roman god who punished oath-breakers in the underworld. His name is the likely source of "ogre" and Tolkien's "orc."
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Zeus: King of the Olympians, god of sky and thunder, not death. His brother Hades got the underworld in a draw.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Apollo: The Greek god of sun, music and healing. Sometimes tied to plague, but not a death god.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Thor: The thunder god of Norse myth, who protects humans, not the dead.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Freya: A Norse goddess of love, who also took half the battle dead to her hall, Folkvangr. Odin took the other half to Valhalla, so she isn't an underworld ruler.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Hestia: Goddess of the hearth and home, the gentlest Olympian, who kept the fire at the heart of every household.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Aphrodite: Goddess of love and beauty, with no underworld role. She was born from sea foam.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Poseidon: The sea god and earth-shaker, so not a ruler of the dead. He's Hades' brother.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Demeter: Goddess of grain and harvest, whose grief at losing her daughter Persephone to the underworld caused winter.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Venus: Roman goddess of love, equal to Aphrodite. Not a goddess of the dead.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Athena: A goddess of wisdom and strategy. No place in the underworld.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Hera: Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage, not tied to death.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Eros: The Greek god of love, whose arrows made people fall for others. Not a god of the dead.
Gods and goddesses of the underworld.Juno: Roman queen of the gods, equal to Hera. She is a goddess of marriage, not of the dead.

Lived in the Middle Ages.Charlemagne: He was crowned emperor on Christmas Day, 800, and united much of western Europe.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Joan of Arc: A peasant girl who led French troops in her teens, was burned in 1431 at about 19, and was made a saint in 1920.
Lived in the Middle Ages.El Cid: A Castilian knight who fought for both Christian and Muslim rulers. His name comes from Arabic for lord.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Genghis Khan: He united the Mongol tribes in 1206, and his successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Marco Polo: The Venetian merchant's travel account of Asia inspired later explorers, and Columbus owned a copy.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Richard Lionheart: This king of England spent only months of his ten-year reign in the country, mostly away on crusade.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Saladin: He retook Jerusalem in 1187 and was admired even by Crusaders for chivalry.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Thomas Aquinas: An Italian friar who blended Aristotle with Christian theology in his Summa Theologica.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Dante: He wrote the Divine Comedy in Tuscan Italian rather than Latin, helping make it the national language.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Chaucer: The Canterbury Tales author helped make English a literary language, and worked as a civil servant.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Robert the Bruce: He was the king who won Scotland's freedom at Bannockburn in 1314. The spider legend is likely a later tale.
Lived in the Middle Ages.William Wallace: The Scottish knight beat the English at Stirling Bridge in 1297 and was executed in 1305.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Kublai Khan: Genghis Khan's grandson, founder of China's Yuan dynasty, and host to Marco Polo.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Julius Caesar: He was assassinated in 44 BC, about five centuries before the Middle Ages are usually said to have begun.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Cleopatra: She lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid, but she was ancient, not medieval.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Shakespeare: He wrote around 1600, in the Renaissance, and his plays often looked back at medieval kings.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Napoleon: He rose to power in the late 1790s and ruled as emperor from 1804, centuries after the medieval era ended.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Elizabeth I: A Tudor queen of the 1500s, in the early modern era, not the Middle Ages.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Isaac Newton: He lived 1643 to 1727, in the scientific revolution, long after the Middle Ages.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Socrates: The Athenian philosopher died in 399 BC, drinking hemlock, nearly 1,500 years before the Middle Ages began.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Alexander the Great: He conquered the Persian Empire in the 300s BC and died at 32, in the ancient world, not the medieval.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Galileo: He lived 1564 to 1642 and used a telescope in 1610, in the early modern age, not the medieval one.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Mozart: An 18th-century composer, from the Classical period and not the medieval one.
Lived in the Middle Ages.Nero: The Roman emperor reigned in the first century AD, in antiquity, centuries before the Middle Ages began.

Things that get hot when you use them.Clothes iron: Early irons were solid chunks of metal heated on a fire; the 'sad iron' name comes from old English 'sad', meaning solid.
Things that get hot when you use them.Toaster: Early electric toasters had exposed wires that scorched bread; the pop-up version arrived in 1919.
Things that get hot when you use them.Oven: Self-cleaning cycles heat the oven to well above 400 C, burning residue to ash.
Things that get hot when you use them.Hair dryer: French hairdresser Alexandre Godefroy invented the first hair dryer for salons around 1890.
Things that get hot when you use them.Kettle: Water boils at 100 C at sea level, but on Everest at only about 70 C.
Things that get hot when you use them.Stove: Benjamin Franklin designed a more efficient wood stove in the 1740s, the Pennsylvania fireplace.
Things that get hot when you use them.Curling iron: Early curling tongs were metal pairs heated in a fire; Marcel Grateau popularized waves with them in the 1870s.
Things that get hot when you use them.Hair straightener: The ceramic or metal plates reach about 150 to 230 C.
Things that get hot when you use them.Space heater: Space heaters are a leading cause of home heating fires, which is why tip-over switches matter.
Things that get hot when you use them.Radiator: Despite its name, most radiators warm a room mostly by convection, not radiation.
Things that get hot when you use them.Waffle maker: The waffle iron was patented in the US in 1869 by Cornelius Swarthout.
Things that get hot when you use them.Glue gun: Hot glue is a thermoplastic that melts at about 120 to 190 C and re-solidifies as it cools.
Things that get hot when you use them.Fridge: A surprise: its back coils release heat, so a fridge warms the kitchen while cooling its insides.
Things that get hot when you use them.Freezer: Freezers hold -18 C as standard, thanks partly to Clarence Birdseye's quick-freezing work in the 1920s.
Things that get hot when you use them.Ice cube tray: Water expands when it freezes by roughly nine percent, which is why trays are flexible.
Things that get hot when you use them.Cooler: Insulation works both ways, so a cooler also keeps hot food warm.
Things that get hot when you use them.Popsicle mold: Frank Epperson reportedly invented the popsicle at age 11 in 1905 by leaving soda and a stick outside overnight.
Things that get hot when you use them.Ice pack: Gel packs stay cold long because gel has high heat capacity, so they absorb warmth slowly.
Things that get hot when you use them.Colander: It drains hot pasta water, but doesn't produce heat; the metal gets warm only from the food.
Things that get hot when you use them.Sponge: Damp sponges harbor bacteria, but they never heat up on their own.
Things that get hot when you use them.Whisk: A whisk only warms from what's in the bowl.
Things that get hot when you use them.Cutting board: Wood boards can have natural antibacterial properties, but they never heat up.
Things that get hot when you use them.Salad spinner: A salad spinner uses centrifugal force and never heats up.
Things that get hot when you use them.Rolling pin: Pastry cooks chill marble rolling pins because the cold keeps butter from melting into dough.

Things that have a blade.Scissors: Scissors are two levers joined at a pivot, and they have existed in some form for over 3,000 years.
Things that have a blade.Razor: Straight razors were sharpened on a leather strop, and a good one could be used for decades.
Things that have a blade.Lawnmower: Edwin Budding built the first mower in 1830 in England, based on a machine that trimmed cloth in textile mills.
Things that have a blade.Blender: A blender's blades are often not very sharp, because it is the high speed, not the edge, that does the chopping.
Things that have a blade.Ceiling fan: The blades are often tilted at about 12 degrees, which is what pushes air downward and makes you feel cooler.
Things that have a blade.Ice skate: A skate blade is hollow ground, with a shallow groove between two edges, giving a skater a grip that glides.
Things that have a blade.Pizza cutter: The rolling pizza wheel is a relatively recent invention, sold widely in the 20th century, and it spares the cheese from dragging.
Things that have a blade.Box cutter: Snap-off blades are scored so you can break off a dull segment, and the idea came from Japanese chocolate broken in sections.
Things that have a blade.Vegetable peeler: A swivel peeler has a blade that flexes and follows the curve of a potato, and it is one of the cheapest handy tools around.
Things that have a blade.Food processor: The blade spins on the base of the bowl, and chefs use the pulse button to avoid turning vegetables into mush.
Things that have a blade.Pencil sharpener: The tiny blade inside is just a sharp piece of steel, set at an angle that shaves wood and graphite into a cone.
Things that have a blade.Spoon: No blade here. A spoon's edge is smooth and rounded, and it is just meant to scoop or stir.
Things that have a blade.Fork: A fork has tines, not blades. They pierce and hold, while a knife does the cutting.
Things that have a blade.Whisk: Wire loops, not blades. A whisk whips air into eggs and cream and does not cut a thing.
Things that have a blade.Hammer: A hammer has a head and a claw, and the claw is for pulling nails, not slicing.
Things that have a blade.Ladle: A ladle has a deep bowl for serving soup, and it has no cutting edge at all.
Things that have a blade.Tongs: Tongs grip food without cutting it, and they work like a pair of levers joined at one end.
Things that have a blade.Rolling pin: It is a smooth cylinder that flattens dough, and a rolling pin with a sharp edge would be a very poor choice.
Things that have a blade.Chopsticks: Chopsticks have no blade at all; they pinch food between two sticks, and that is why food is cut into bite-size pieces in the kitchen.
Things that have a blade.Stapler: A stapler drives a metal staple through paper, using a spring and a small steel plate rather than a cutting edge.
Things that have a blade.Paintbrush: It carries paint on its bristles, which are soft and blunt, and a brush has nothing to cut with.
Things that have a blade.Comb: A comb has teeth, not blades, and its job is to separate and align hair rather than cut it.
Things that have a blade.Toothbrush: Its bristles are soft nylon, which is a long way from a blade, and tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the body.
Things that have a blade.Spatula: A spatula slides under food to lift or flip it; its edge is flat and thin but is not designed to cut.

Things that have a head.Hammer: A hammer's head is the heavy striking part; most are made of forged steel, and the claw on the other side pulls nails.
Things that have a head.Nail: A nail's flat head gives you something to hit, and nails once were hand-forged one at a time until machines took over in the 1800s.
Things that have a head.Screw: A screw's head comes in many drive types, such as slotted, Phillips, and Torx, and each was designed to improve grip.
Things that have a head.Sewing pin: A sewing pin has a small round head so it's easy to push and so it won't slip all the way through the fabric.
Things that have a head.Match: A match's head contains chemicals that ignite with friction, and safety matches only light when struck on the special strip.
Things that have a head.Lettuce: A head of lettuce is a tight ball of leaves, and the plant is a relative of the sunflower, with ancient Egyptian roots.
Things that have a head.Cabbage: A head of cabbage can be bred into broccoli, kale, and cauliflower, since all are the same species.
Things that have a head.Golf club: A golf club's head is the part that hits the ball, and modern ones are often made of titanium for light weight and size.
Things that have a head.Shower: A shower head sprays water out of dozens of small holes, and low-flow ones use less than 2 gallons a minute.
Things that have a head.Mop: A mop head is a bundle of cloth or yarn strands, and the first mop designs date back to the 1800s.
Things that have a head.Toothbrush: A toothbrush head holds the bristles, and dentists suggest replacing it about every three months, or sooner if it's frayed.
Things that have a head.Garlic: A head of garlic is a bulb made of cloves, and ancient Egyptian workers building pyramids reportedly ate it for strength.
Things that have a head.Ruler: A ruler is a straight strip with marks; it has an end but no head, and the word 'rule' comes from the Latin for 'straight stick'.
Things that have a head.Rope: A rope has two ends and a middle, but no head, and the ends are often 'whipped' with twine to stop them from fraying.
Things that have a head.Brick: A brick has faces, ends, and edges, and builders call its long side the stretcher and short end the header, which is not a head.
Things that have a head.Sock: A sock has a cuff, leg, heel, and toe, but no head, which is why it's a good example of what doesn't have one.
Things that have a head.Plate: A plate has a rim and a well, but no head, though it does have a 'face' in the language of dishware.
Things that have a head.Towel: A towel has hems and loops, but no head, though some bath towels have a hood that's actually for the head.
Things that have a head.Banana: A banana grows in a hand, with individual fruits called fingers, but it has no head and the plant is technically an herb.
Things that have a head.Carrot: A carrot is a root with a leafy top and no head, though the greens at the top are edible and sometimes used for pesto.
Things that have a head.Potato: A potato has eyes, which are the buds from which new plants grow, but it doesn't have a head.
Things that have a head.Envelope: An envelope has a flap, a back, and a seal, but no head, though the top part is sometimes called the 'head' by printers.
Things that have a head.Ladder: A ladder has rails and rungs, and no head, though the very top rung of a stepladder is where it says not to stand.
Things that have a head.Pencil: A pencil has a lead, a ferrule, and an eraser, not a head, although the eraser tip is sometimes called its 'head'.

Parts of a shoe.Sole: The sole is the bottom of the shoe, and the first ones were wood or leather, with rubber soles only coming around in the 1800s.
Parts of a shoe.Heel: The heel gives lift, and high heels were originally worn by Persian horse riders to keep their feet in the stirrups.
Parts of a shoe.Tongue: The tongue sits under the laces and protects your foot from lace pressure.
Parts of a shoe.Laces: Laces are tied with a shoelace knot, and a granny knot, as opposed to a reef knot, comes undone more often.
Parts of a shoe.Insole: The insole is the inner layer that cushions your foot, and it can be swapped out for extra comfort.
Parts of a shoe.Eyelet: Eyelets are the holes where laces pass, and they're often reinforced with metal rings to prevent tearing.
Parts of a shoe.Toe cap: A toe cap protects toes, and steel toe boots can handle thousands of pounds of force.
Parts of a shoe.Aglet: An aglet is the little plastic or metal tip on a lace, and the word comes from the Latin for needle.
Parts of a shoe.Outsole: The outsole is the part touching the ground, and its tread is designed for grip.
Parts of a shoe.Sleeve: A sleeve covers an arm in a shirt or coat, so it's clothing, not footwear, though some boots do have a long shaft.
Parts of a shoe.Brim: A brim is the rim of a hat that shades the face, and a wide one can block much of the sun's UV.
Parts of a shoe.Lens: A lens belongs to glasses or a camera, and the word comes from the Latin for lentil because of its shape.
Parts of a shoe.Wick: A wick is the cord that draws melted wax up a candle, and so it belongs to a candle, not a shoe.
Parts of a shoe.Spout: A spout belongs to a kettle or teapot, where it pours liquid, and a shoe has no need to pour.
Parts of a shoe.Hinge: A hinge lets a door or lid swing, and hinges are among the oldest hardware, found in ancient Egypt.
Parts of a shoe.Pocket: A pocket is sewn into trousers or a jacket, and until the 1800s women often wore theirs as a separate tied pouch.
Parts of a shoe.Lapel: A lapel is the folded flap on a jacket's chest, and a buttonhole there was once used for a boutonniere flower.
Parts of a shoe.Visor: A visor is the peak of a cap or helmet, and it shades the eyes, so it sits on a head instead of a foot.
Parts of a shoe.Cufflink: A cufflink fastens a shirt cuff, so it's an accessory for wrists, and it was once a status symbol of the wealthy.
Parts of a shoe.Waistband: A waistband holds up trousers or skirts at the middle of the body, a long way up from the shoe.
Parts of a shoe.Hood: A hood covers the head on a coat or sweatshirt, and some medieval hoods were worn by monks and workers alike.
Parts of a shoe.Lid: A lid covers a pot, jar or box, and it's one part that no shoe has, since a shoe stays open at the top.
Parts of a shoe.Handle: A handle is part of a bag, cup or door, but a shoe is carried by your foot and has none.
Parts of a shoe.Bristles: Bristles are the stiff hairs of a brush, though a shoe brush is what makes your shoes shine, not part of the shoe.

Things that stink.Skunk: A skunk's spray comes from glands near the tail, and its smell is mainly sulfur compounds called thiols, detectable from far away.
Things that stink.Garbage: Garbage smells bad because bacteria breaking down food release sulfur compounds and other gases.
Things that stink.Rotten egg: The rotten-egg smell is hydrogen sulfide, and we can detect it at tiny concentrations, a built-in warning.
Things that stink.Old socks: Foot smell comes from bacteria feeding on sweat, and socks keep the party going.
Things that stink.Sewer: Sewer gas smells largely of hydrogen sulfide, which at high concentrations dulls your nose's ability to detect it.
Things that stink.Dirty diaper: Babies' diapers smell strong because of bacteria digesting waste, and the odor changes as their diet changes.
Things that stink.Sour milk: Milk sours when bacteria turn lactose into lactic acid, which makes it curdle.
Things that stink.Wet dog: Wet dog smell comes from microorganisms on the fur releasing smelly compounds as water evaporates.
Things that stink.Spoiled fish: Fish smells fishy as it spoils because bacteria produce trimethylamine.
Things that stink.Stinky feet: Each foot has around 125,000 sweat glands, but it's the bacteria on the sweat that make the smell.
Things that stink.Landfill: Landfills release methane and hydrogen sulfide as trash breaks down, and the gas is often collected for energy.
Things that stink.Roses: Making a single kilogram of rose oil takes several tonnes of petals, which makes it enormously expensive.
Things that stink.Fresh bread: The smell of baking bread comes from hundreds of compounds made as sugars and amino acids react in the crust.
Things that stink.Lavender: Lavender oil's scent comes largely from linalool, and studies suggest it can calm anxiety slightly.
Things that stink.Vanilla: Vanilla comes from an orchid's seed pods, and it's often called the second most expensive spice after saffron.
Things that stink.Clean laundry: The clean laundry smell comes largely from added fragrance, since truly clean fabric has little smell at all.
Things that stink.Cinnamon: Cinnamon is dried tree bark, and its scent comes from a compound called cinnamaldehyde.
Things that stink.Fresh coffee: Coffee's aroma comes from hundreds of compounds, and one of them, a thiol, smells like skunk in its pure form.
Things that stink.Pine tree: Pine scent comes from pinene, which also helps trees repel insects.
Things that stink.Baby powder: Baby powder's scent is added fragrance, since talc and cornstarch themselves are nearly odorless.
Things that stink.Lilac: Lilac flowers can't be distilled for scent, so perfumers recreate it from other ingredients.
Things that stink.Popcorn: Popcorn's smell comes from a compound called 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, which is also found in basmati rice and bread crust.
Things that stink.Lemon zest: The zest's fragrant oils sit in tiny sacs in the peel, which burst when you grate it.
Things that stink.Cookies: Real estate agents famously bake cookies before showings, since the warm smell makes homes feel welcoming.

Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Chocolate: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs process slowly, and dark chocolate is the most dangerous kind.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Grapes: Grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, yet vets still don't know exactly which compound is responsible.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Raisins: Raisins are even more concentrated than grapes, so a small handful can be harmful to a small dog.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Onions: Onions damage a dog's red blood cells and cooked or powdered onions are still toxic, so avoid onion-flavored baby food too.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Garlic: Garlic is related to onion and in larger amounts is toxic to dogs, and it's harmful in cooked or powdered form too.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Xylitol gum: Xylitol, a sweetener in many gums, can cause a dog's blood sugar to crash within minutes, and is very dangerous even in tiny amounts.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Macadamia nuts: Macadamia nuts can make dogs weak, wobbly and feverish, though scientists still can't say which compound causes it.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Coffee: Coffee contains caffeine, which dogs are quite sensitive to, so even spilled grounds are a worry.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Cooked chicken bones: Cooked bones turn brittle and can splinter, which risks cuts or blockages in a dog's gut, unlike raw ones.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Avocado pit: An avocado pit is a choking and blockage hazard, and the plant contains persin, which is a mild toxin for many animals.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Carrots: Carrots are a safe, crunchy snack, and many dogs adore them; they're low in calories, too.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Plain rice: Plain cooked rice is a vet-recommended bland food for dogs with an upset stomach, often paired with chicken.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Apple slices: Apple slices are safe for dogs once the core and seeds are removed, and they're crunchy and sweet.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Blueberries: Blueberries are safe for dogs, and they're rich in antioxidants, and are a popular low-calorie treat.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Plain chicken: Plain cooked chicken is a staple of dog diets, as long as there is no seasoning, skin fat or bones.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Pumpkin: Plain pumpkin is full of fiber, which is why vets suggest a spoonful for dogs with digestive troubles.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Green beans: Green beans are a low-calorie filler, and some vets suggest them to help overweight dogs feel fuller.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Dog kibble: Kibble was invented in the early 1900s, and a complete dog food formulated for balanced nutrition is the safest choice.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Sweet potato: Sweet potato is a safe, fiber-rich dog treat, as long as it is cooked and served plain.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Banana: Bananas are safe and potassium-rich for dogs, but their sugar means they're best as an occasional treat.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Cucumber: Cucumber is about 95 percent water and has very few calories, which makes it a great dog treat.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Plain turkey: Plain cooked turkey is fine for dogs, but the skin, seasoning and fat can lead to stomach trouble.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Dog biscuit: Dog biscuits date to the 1860s, when an American electrician in London, James Spratt, began selling them to dogs.
Things you shouldn't feed a dog.Seedless watermelon: Seedless watermelon is safe and hydrating for dogs, but remove the rind and any seeds first.

Things a fisherman uses.Fishing rod: Rods have long been made of bamboo, and later fiberglass and carbon fiber made them light and strong.
Things a fisherman uses.Reel: A reel stores and winds the line, and the first reels were used in China about a thousand years ago.
Things a fisherman uses.Hook: Hooks date back tens of thousands of years, and early ones were made of bone, shell or wood.
Things a fisherman uses.Bait: Bait is anything that tempts a fish, from worms and insects to bread and cheese.
Things a fisherman uses.Net: Nets can catch fish in bulk, and a trawl net may be large enough to hold several airplanes.
Things a fisherman uses.Lure: A lure imitates prey with color, shape and motion, and some even have flashing metal like a fish scale.
Things a fisherman uses.Tackle box: A tackle box holds hooks, lures and sinkers, and keen anglers often own plenty of them.
Things a fisherman uses.Waders: Waders are waterproof overalls that keep an angler dry while standing in a river up to the chest.
Things a fisherman uses.Sinker: A sinker is a weight that carries the line down, and lead was once common, though it's now often replaced due to toxicity.
Things a fisherman uses.Bobber: A bobber floats on the water and dips when a fish bites, which signals the angler to react.
Things a fisherman uses.Fishing line: Modern line is often nylon or braided and can be nearly invisible underwater, which helps fool wary fish.
Things a fisherman uses.Lasso: A lasso catches cattle on land, and a fisherman's rope is more likely a mooring line on a boat.
Things a fisherman uses.Saddle: A saddle is for horses, and while fishermen may ride boats, they certainly don't use one at sea.
Things a fisherman uses.Butterfly net: A butterfly net is for insects, and fish need a much stronger one.
Things a fisherman uses.Bee smoker: A smoker calms bees and has no place on a fishing trip.
Things a fisherman uses.Pitchfork: A pitchfork moves hay on a farm, though the three-pronged fish spear called a leister looks a bit like it.
Things a fisherman uses.Plough: A plough turns the soil on a farm, and the sea has no soil to turn, though trawlers do plough the seabed.
Things a fisherman uses.Spurs: Spurs are worn by riders, so they're a horseman's gear.
Things a fisherman uses.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's tool for listening to hearts.
Things a fisherman uses.Easel: An easel is for a painter's canvas, not a rod.
Things a fisherman uses.Kiln: A kiln is a potter's oven that fires clay at over a thousand degrees, a far cry from the cold waters of a lake.
Things a fisherman uses.Chisel: A chisel is for carving, a carpenter's tool.
Things a fisherman uses.Briefcase: A briefcase is for office papers, and fish don't care about meetings.
Things a fisherman uses.Ice skates: Ice skates are for gliding, though ice fishers do walk on frozen lakes to fish through holes.

Things a butcher uses.Cleaver: A cleaver is thick and heavy enough to chop through bone, which is why butchers rely on it.
Things a butcher uses.Meat hook: Meat hooks let carcasses hang for dry-ageing, which makes beef more tender and intense in flavour.
Things a butcher uses.Bone saw: A butcher's bone saw cuts through ribs and joints, and band saws do the same in large shops.
Things a butcher uses.Butcher's block: Traditional butcher's blocks are made from thick end-grain wood such as maple, which resists knife marks.
Things a butcher uses.Meat grinder: Grinding mince at home lets you pick the cut, and a butcher's grinder turns trimmings into minced beef or sausage meat.
Things a butcher uses.Boning knife: A boning knife has a narrow, flexible blade that slips along bones to remove meat cleanly.
Things a butcher uses.Sharpening steel: A steel doesn't truly sharpen a knife so much as realign its edge, since real sharpening needs a stone.
Things a butcher uses.Weighing scale: Butchers weigh meat to sell it by weight, and legal-for-trade scales must be checked and certified.
Things a butcher uses.Apron: Blue-and-white striped aprons are the classic butcher's look in Britain, and they hide stains better than plain white.
Things a butcher uses.Butcher's twine: Butcher's twine ties roasts so they cook evenly and keep their shape.
Things a butcher uses.Sausage stuffer: Sausages are filled into casings, traditionally cleaned animal intestines, and a stuffer pushes the meat in.
Things a butcher uses.Whisk: A whisk adds air to eggs and cream, which makes it a baker's and cook's tool, not a butcher's.
Things a butcher uses.Piping bag: A piping bag decorates cakes with icing, which is pastry chef territory.
Things a butcher uses.Cake tin: A cake tin shapes a sponge in the oven, and so it belongs in a bakery, not in a butcher's shop.
Things a butcher uses.Tamper: A tamper presses coffee grounds, a barista's tool, and isn't for compressing meat.
Things a butcher uses.Cookie cutter: A cookie cutter stamps shapes into dough, so bakers use it and butchers don't.
Things a butcher uses.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough, not meat, since meat is pounded with a mallet.
Things a butcher uses.Pastry brush: A pastry brush glazes pastry with egg wash or butter, and butchers have no use for one.
Things a butcher uses.Melon baller: A melon baller scoops round balls out of fruit, which is a fruit-bowl job, not a butcher's.
Things a butcher uses.Egg timer: An egg timer times boiled eggs, and the classic one is a sand-filled hourglass.
Things a butcher uses.Tea strainer: A tea strainer catches loose leaves, which is nothing a butcher needs.
Things a butcher uses.Garlic press: A garlic press crushes cloves, and a butcher wouldn't use one.
Things a butcher uses.Ice cream scoop: An ice cream scoop portions frozen dessert, and the first patented one came in 1897 from Alfred Cralle.
Things a butcher uses.Sushi mat: A sushi mat rolls rice and nori into maki, so it's a sushi chef's tool.

Things a potter makes.Vase: Ancient Greek potters painted vases with myths and daily life, and those scenes are a main source for what we know of Greek society.
Things a potter makes.Mug: Many potters pull a mug's handle from a lump of wet clay, stretching it like taffy, then attach it before the body dries.
Things a potter makes.Bowl: Pottery bowls from East Asia are about 20,000 years old, making them among the oldest ceramics and older than farming.
Things a potter makes.Plate: Wide, flat plates warp and crack easily, so potters often dry them slowly under cover before they ever reach the kiln.
Things a potter makes.Teapot: Yixing teapots from China are made of unglazed purple clay, and tea lovers say the pot absorbs flavor with years of use.
Things a potter makes.Jug: A jug's narrow neck is made by squeezing the spinning clay inward, a step potters call collaring.
Things a potter makes.Urn: Keats wrote an ode to a Grecian urn, but real Greek urns were everyday pots for storing ashes, wine or grain.
Things a potter makes.Flowerpot: Terracotta pots are left unglazed on purpose: the porous clay lets roots breathe and extra moisture evaporate.
Things a potter makes.Ceramic tiles: Portugal's painted azulejo tiles have covered walls for centuries, and fired clay tiles can survive thousands of years.
Things a potter makes.Basket: A basket is woven from reeds or willow, not shaped from clay. Basketry and pottery are both ancient, but separate crafts.
Things a potter makes.Horseshoe: Horseshoes are forged from iron by a farrier at a hot forge, so they belong to the blacksmith's trade, not the potter's.
Things a potter makes.Quilt: Quilts are stitched layers of fabric made with needle and thread. No wheel, clay or kiln is involved, so the quilter owns this one.
Things a potter makes.Candle: Candles come from wax poured or dipped around a wick. Their makers were called chandlers, not potters.
Things a potter makes.Sweater: A sweater is knitted from yarn, a textile craft. A potter works with wet clay, so this one is a trap.
Things a potter makes.Rope: Rope is made by twisting fibers into strands, then twisting the strands together. That is a ropemaker's job.
Things a potter makes.Saddle: Saddles are leatherwork: a saddler stitches leather over a wooden frame called a tree. Clay has no part in it.
Things a potter makes.Wig: Wigs are made by hand-knotting hair strand by strand onto a net base, a wigmaker's craft with no clay involved.
Things a potter makes.Barrel: A barrel is built by a cooper, who bends wooden staves with heat and locks them with iron hoops, using no glue.
Things a potter makes.Broom: Brooms are bound from straw or bristles by a broom maker. A potter might use one for sweeping up clay dust.
Things a potter makes.Hat: Hats belong to the hatter or milliner. The phrase 'mad as a hatter' is often linked to mercury once used in felt making.
Things a potter makes.Belt: Belts are cut from leather and fitted with a buckle, the trade of a leatherworker rather than a potter.
Things a potter makes.Shoes: Shoes are the cobbler's work. The oldest known leather shoe, found in an Armenian cave, is about 5,500 years old.
Things a potter makes.Soap: Soap is made by mixing fat with lye, a reaction called saponification. It belongs to the soapmaker, not the potter.
Things a potter makes.Kite: Kites are made from a light frame and paper or cloth, and were probably invented in China over 2,000 years ago.

Military unit names.Squad: A squad is about eight to twelve soldiers, usually led by a sergeant, and is a basic building block of an army.
Military unit names.Platoon: A platoon is usually 20 to 50 soldiers led by a lieutenant, and the word comes from French 'peloton', a little ball.
Military unit names.Company: A company is usually 100 to 200 soldiers led by a captain, and several companies make a battalion.
Military unit names.Battalion: A battalion usually has several hundred soldiers, commonly 300 to 1,000, and is often led by a lieutenant colonel.
Military unit names.Regiment: Regiments carry deep tradition and have their own colors and history, and some British ones date to the 1600s.
Military unit names.Brigade: A brigade is a few thousand troops, built from several battalions. It is also the Light Brigade of Tennyson's poem.
Military unit names.Division: A division usually has 10,000 to 20,000 soldiers, the first level that combines infantry, artillery and support.
Military unit names.Corps: A corps is made of two or more divisions. The word is pronounced 'core' and comes from the French for 'body'.
Military unit names.Troop: Troop is the cavalry's equivalent of a company, and 'troops' also means soldiers in general.
Military unit names.Fireteam: A fireteam is typically four soldiers, the smallest maneuver unit and about half of a squad.
Military unit names.Squadron: A squadron is a unit of cavalry or air forces, and also a group of warships, so the word has three military uses.
Military unit names.Fleet: A fleet is a large naval unit of many ships. The US Navy has numbered fleets, like the Seventh Fleet in the Pacific.
Military unit names.Flock: A flock is a group of birds or sheep. It's a collective noun for animals, so it doesn't fit as a military unit.
Military unit names.Herd: A herd is a group of cattle, deer or elephants. Armies might feel herded, but a herd isn't a military unit.
Military unit names.Swarm: A swarm is a mass of insects, like bees or locusts. Drone 'swarms' are a modern idea, but no army formally uses the word.
Military unit names.Pride: A pride is a group of lions, one of the best-known collective nouns for animals. It isn't a military unit.
Military unit names.Gaggle: A gaggle is a group of geese on the ground. In flight they become a skein, and neither is a military unit.
Military unit names.Pod: A pod is a group of whales or dolphins. It isn't a military term, though a submarine crew might disagree.
Military unit names.Murder: A murder is a group of crows, one of the best-known collective nouns. It isn't a military unit.
Military unit names.Litter: A litter is a group of newborn animals, like puppies or kittens, and nothing to do with an army.
Military unit names.Troupe: Troupe sounds like troop, which is the trap. It means a group of performers, not soldiers.
Military unit names.Bevy: A bevy is a group of quail or other birds, and also of ladies. It sounds grand, but isn't a military word.
Military unit names.Parliament: A group of owls is called a parliament, which is a collective noun for animals, not an army unit.
Military unit names.Clutch: A clutch is a set of eggs laid in one nest. It isn't a military term, although a clutch of recruits is plausible.

NATO alphabet words from N to Z.November: November is N, the 14th letter. Words like this were picked to be understandable in many languages over a bad radio link.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Oscar: Oscar stands for O, and is also the nickname of the golden Academy Award statuette, whose official name is the Academy Award of Merit.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Papa: Papa stands for P, and is pronounced 'PAH-PAH' in the official respelling, with stress on both syllables.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Quebec: Quebec stands for Q, and is pronounced 'keh-BECK', as in French, rather than the usual English way.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Romeo: Romeo stands for R, and Shakespeare's lover has a partner elsewhere in the alphabet: Juliett, spelled with two t's.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Sierra: Sierra stands for S, and is Spanish for a jagged 'mountain range', as in the Sierra Nevada.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Tango: Tango stands for T, and is also the Argentine and Uruguayan dance that UNESCO lists as cultural heritage.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Uniform: Uniform stands for U, and the official pronunciation can be 'YOU-nee-form' or 'OO-nee-form'.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Victor: Victor stands for V, and is a Latin name meaning 'winner', which suits a word built for clarity over radio.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Whiskey: Whiskey stands for W, and is spelled with an 'e' in the official alphabet, the Irish and American way.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.X-ray: X-ray is the only hyphenated word in the alphabet, and stands for X. It's a spelling quirk worth remembering.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Yankee: Yankee stands for Y, a word historically used for people from the northern US or New England.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Zulu: Zulu ends the alphabet, and is also the name of a large Southern African people and their language.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Alpha: Alpha is the first letter, A, so it belongs to the first half. The official spelling is actually 'Alfa'.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Bravo: Bravo stands for B, so it belongs to the first half of the alphabet, and not the N to Z half.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Delta: Delta stands for D, so it falls in the first half. It's also a Greek letter and a river's fan-shaped mouth.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Golf: Golf stands for G, in the first half of the alphabet, and shares its name with the sport played with clubs.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Hotel: Hotel stands for H, early in the alphabet, so it falls in the first half, not the N to Z half.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Kilo: Kilo stands for K, and is short for 'kilogram' in everyday speech, but it still belongs to the first half.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Lima: Lima stands for L, so it's in the first half. It's also the capital of Peru, which sounds the same.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Mike: Mike stands for M, the 13th letter, so it's just one short of the N to Z half. It's also a common name.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Roger: Roger was the old WWII word for R, replaced by Romeo, though 'roger that' lives on as radio slang for 'received'.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Sugar: Sugar was the old WWII word for S, which was replaced by Sierra when the alphabet was standardized in the 1950s.
NATO alphabet words from N to Z.Uncle: Uncle was the wartime word for U, long since replaced by Uniform in the modern international alphabet.

Video streaming services.Hulu: Hulu launched in 2007 as a joint venture of broadcasters and is now majority owned by Disney.
Video streaming services.Disney+: Disney+ launched in November 2019 and signed up millions of users on its first day.
Video streaming services.HBO Max: HBO Max launched in 2020 and later was rebranded as Max and then back to HBO Max.
Video streaming services.Prime Video: Prime Video comes with Amazon Prime membership and began as Amazon Unbox in 2006.
Video streaming services.Peacock: Peacock is NBCUniversal's service, named for the network's colorful peacock logo.
Video streaming services.Paramount+: Paramount+ replaced CBS All Access in 2021 and streams Star Trek shows.
Video streaming services.Crunchyroll: Crunchyroll began as an anime fan site in 2006 and is now a leading anime streaming service.
Video streaming services.Tubi: Tubi offers a large library of free movies and shows paid by ads, and it is owned by Fox.
Video streaming services.Pluto TV: Pluto TV shows free channels that mimic cable TV, and it's owned by Paramount.
Video streaming services.Spotify: Spotify is mostly a music and podcast service, so it doesn't count as a video streaming service despite some video content.
Video streaming services.Pandora: Pandora is a music service famous for its Music Genome Project radio stations, so it's audio rather than video.
Video streaming services.SoundCloud: SoundCloud is an audio platform built around independent musicians and remixes, not video.
Video streaming services.Audible: Audible sells audiobooks and is owned by Amazon, but it's audio only, unlike Amazon's Prime Video.
Video streaming services.Duolingo: Duolingo teaches languages through short lessons, and its green owl mascot is known for guilt-trip reminders.
Video streaming services.Deezer: Deezer is a French music streaming service launched in 2007, so it's about songs rather than shows.
Video streaming services.Kindle: Amazon's Kindle is for reading ebooks; it has no video library, unlike Prime Video from the same company.
Video streaming services.Shazam: Shazam identifies songs by their audio fingerprint, and Apple bought it in 2018; it doesn't stream video.
Video streaming services.Napster: Napster began in 1999 as a music file-sharing network, was shut down by lawsuits, and later returned as a legal music service.
Video streaming services.Last.fm: Last.fm records what you listen to, a habit called scrobbling, and recommends music, so it's about audio only.
Video streaming services.iHeartRadio: iHeartRadio streams radio stations and podcasts, which makes it audio, not video.
Video streaming services.Apple Music: Apple Music launched in 2015 for songs and music videos, but it's primarily a music service, unlike Apple TV+.
Video streaming services.Audacity: Audacity is a free audio editor, not a streaming service, and it's popular among podcasters.
Video streaming services.Goodreads: Goodreads is a book review community that Amazon bought in 2013; it has no videos to stream.

Game franchises owned by Sony.The Last of Us: Naughty Dog's survival drama borrows from the real Cordyceps fungus, which infects insects, and it became an acclaimed HBO series.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Horizon: Guerrilla's open-world series pits a hunter against robot dinosaurs. Guerrilla, a Dutch studio, was previously known mainly for Killzone.

Game franchises owned by Sony.Ghost of Tsushima: Sucker Punch's 2020 samurai epic is set in the 1274 Mongol invasion, and it also lets players view the game in a black-and-white Kurosawa mode.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Killzone: Guerrilla's sci-fi shooter series about the Helghast was once pitched as a 'Halo killer' for the PlayStation 2.
Game franchises owned by Sony.LittleBigPlanet: Media Molecule's 2008 platformer starred a customizable Sackboy and invited players to build and share their own levels with the motto 'Play, Create, Share'.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Sly Cooper: Sucker Punch's stealth platformers star a raccoon thief from a long line of burglars, and the studio later made Ghost of Tsushima.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Jak and Daxter: Naughty Dog's 2001 platformer ran without visible loading screens, a technical feat that was rare at the time on the PlayStation 2.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Halo: A Microsoft series, and since Microsoft bought Bungie in 2000 it's been Xbox's flagship, so it doesn't belong to Sony.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Gears of War: An Xbox-exclusive shooter series, and Microsoft bought it from Epic in 2014, so it isn't Sony's.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Forza: Turn 10's Xbox racing games count hundreds of cars, and they're Microsoft-owned, not Sony's.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Fable: A British role-playing series from Lionhead, owned by Microsoft, though the studio closed in 2016. Not Sony.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Mario: Nintendo's plumber has never been Sony's, though he is probably the best-known video game character in history.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Zelda: Nintendo's franchise. A Sony console has never hosted the series, and these games stay with Nintendo.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Metroid: Nintendo's, and the series is rare for starring a woman, Samus Aran, who stars in games on Nintendo consoles only.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Kirby: A Nintendo mascot, developed by HAL Laboratory, so he's not owned by Sony. His creator Masahiro Sakurai also directed Smash Bros.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Splatoon: A Nintendo shooter whose characters shoot paint and turn into squids, and it's Nintendo's, not Sony's.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Sonic: Sega's blue hedgehog was Mario's old rival and Sega once fought Sony's PlayStation in the console wars, so he isn't Sony's.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Crash Bandicoot: A trap: Crash began as a PlayStation mascot in 1996, but Sony never owned him. Activision, and so Microsoft, owns Crash now.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Spyro: Another early PlayStation mascot that Sony never owned: Activision does, which means it is now part of Microsoft's stable.
Game franchises owned by Sony.Pac-Man: Bandai Namco's yellow chomper came out in 1980 in arcades, and it has never belonged to Sony.

Camera brands.Canon: Founded in Japan in the 1930s, the company was first called Kwanon after a Buddhist goddess of mercy, and it leads the market in cameras.
Camera brands.Nikon: Its F-series cameras were famous with photojournalists, and Nikon lenses even went to the Moon on Apollo missions.
Camera brands.Sony: It bought Konica Minolta's camera business in 2006 and now leads in mirrorless cameras with its Alpha line.
Camera brands.Fujifilm: Famed for its color film, it survived the digital age by reinventing itself, and it now also makes cosmetics and medicine.
Camera brands.Olympus: Known first for microscopes, it sold its camera business in 2021 to a new company, OM Digital Solutions, which keeps the Olympus name.
Camera brands.Leica: The 1925 Leica I made small 35 mm film cameras popular, and photographers like Henri Cartier-Bresson used it for street photography.
Camera brands.Kodak: Founder George Eastman coined the name in 1888 partly because he liked the letter K. The company's slogan was 'You press the button, we do the rest'.
Camera brands.Pentax: The Japanese brand had a long history of building cameras with robust bodies, and it's now owned by Ricoh.
Camera brands.Polaroid: Edwin Land's 1948 instant camera developed pictures in about a minute, and the company's film is still made today.
Camera brands.GoPro: Founder Nick Woodman started it after surfing, building a camera for athletes, and it became a hit for action footage.
Camera brands.Hasselblad: This Swedish brand's cameras took photographs on the Moon in 1969, and astronauts left most of the bodies there.
Camera brands.Panasonic: Its Lumix G1 of 2008 was the first mirrorless interchangeable-lens camera, though Panasonic is much bigger in electronics and batteries.
Camera brands.Bose: A trap: Bose makes audio equipment, famed for noise-cancelling headphones, and it's not a camera brand.
Camera brands.Yamaha: It started with pianos and organs in 1887 and now makes instruments and motorcycles, but not cameras.
Camera brands.Nvidia: Famous for graphics chips that power games and AI, it doesn't make cameras, though its GPUs process the photos from many.
Camera brands.Intel: Its processors are inside countless PCs, but it doesn't make cameras, even if its chips process the pictures that they take.
Camera brands.Fitbit: Maker of fitness trackers and now part of Google, so it's a wearable brand rather than a camera maker.
Camera brands.Spotify: Founded in Sweden in 2006, this music-streaming service sells songs, not photographs, and it makes no cameras.
Camera brands.Seagate: It makes hard drives that store your photos, but not the cameras that take them, so it doesn't fit.
Camera brands.Netgear: This company builds routers and networking gear, so it doesn't make cameras, though it did once sell Arlo security cameras.
Camera brands.Adobe: The maker of Photoshop edits photos, but it doesn't build cameras. Its name comes from a creek behind a founder's house.
Camera brands.Oracle: A database and cloud company, not a camera brand. It was named for a CIA project that its founders worked on.
Camera brands.JBL: A speaker brand famed for its concert and car audio, not for cameras. It's named after founder James B. Lansing.
Camera brands.Sennheiser: A German audio company known for headphones and microphones, and it makes no cameras.

Facebook features.Like: Introduced in 2009, the thumbs-up button was nearly named Awesome internally, and expanded into reactions in 2016.
Facebook features.Wall: Facebook's original profile space where friends posted messages was replaced by Timeline in 2011.
Facebook features.News Feed: Launched in 2006, it triggered a user revolt over privacy before becoming the heart of Facebook.
Facebook features.Marketplace: Launched in 2016, it lets people buy and sell locally, and quickly became one of the biggest classified sites.
Facebook features.Groups: Communities around interests, from neighborhoods to hobbies, some having millions of members.
Facebook features.Events: A way to host and RSVP to gatherings; it replaced traditional paper invitations for many users.
Facebook features.Timeline: The 2011 redesign of the profile that arranges a person's life story by date, replacing the old Wall.
Facebook features.Messenger: Facebook's chat service, which became a standalone app in 2011 and later reached a billion users.
Facebook features.Status update: The short posts that began, in the early days, with your name and the word is, now simply shared.
Facebook features.Friend request: The invitation that builds Facebook's social graph, and the way to connect, and fear of rejection.
Facebook features.Pages: Public profiles for brands, artists and businesses, separate from personal profiles.
Facebook features.Retweet: A repost on Twitter, now X, that spreads a tweet to your followers; Facebook uses Share instead.
Facebook features.Snap: Snapchat's disappearing photo message gave the app its name, and its ghost logo.
Facebook features.Streak: Snapchat counts consecutive days of messaging with a flame emoji, which keeps teens glued.
Facebook features.Upvote: Reddit's way of boosting a post, and not a Facebook thing, which uses Like.
Facebook features.Karma: Reddit's score for contributions, earned from upvotes, which has no equivalent on Facebook.
Facebook features.Subreddit: A topic-based community on Reddit, written as r/ followed by a name.
Facebook features.Duet: TikTok lets you create a side-by-side video with another user's clip.
Facebook features.Stitch: A TikTok feature that clips part of another video and adds your reply after it.
Facebook features.Repin: Pinterest's way of saving someone else's pin to your own board.
Facebook features.Swipe right: The Tinder gesture meaning you like someone; it spread into everyday slang for choosing.
Facebook features.Superlike: A Tinder extra that signals strong interest, and users get only a few for free per day.
Facebook features.Fleet: Twitter's short-lived disappearing posts, launched in 2020 and quietly retired in 2021.

Characters in Great Expectations.Pip: Orphan Philip Pirrip narrates the story and shortened his own name to Pip as a child because he couldn't say it properly.
Characters in Great Expectations.Estella: Raised by Miss Havisham to break men's hearts, she turns out to be the secret daughter of the convict Magwitch.
Characters in Great Expectations.Miss Havisham: Jilted at the altar, she stopped every clock at twenty to nine and kept her rotting wedding cake for decades.
Characters in Great Expectations.Joe Gargery: The gentle village blacksmith is Pip's brother-in-law and truest friend, a model of simple, unshowy goodness.
Characters in Great Expectations.Magwitch: The escaped convict Pip helps on the marshes in chapter one later turns out to be his secret benefactor.
Characters in Great Expectations.Herbert Pocket: Pip's cheerful friend teaches him table manners in London and nicknames him Handel, after the composer.
Characters in Great Expectations.Jaggers: The formidable criminal lawyer constantly washes his hands and cross-examines everyone, even friends, as though in court.
Characters in Great Expectations.Wemmick: Jaggers's clerk is cold at work, but at home he is warm, with a tiny castle-like house with a drawbridge, a cannon and his deaf father.
Characters in Great Expectations.Biddy: Pip's kind, sensible village friend sees through his snobbery and ends up marrying Joe, a better match than Pip deserved.
Characters in Great Expectations.Orlick: The surly journeyman at the forge attacks Pip's sister with a leg-iron and later tries to murder Pip himself.
Characters in Great Expectations.Pumblechook: Joe's pompous uncle, a corn merchant, loudly claims credit for Pip's rise and is one of Dickens's great comic windbags.
Characters in Great Expectations.Compeyson: The smooth swindler who jilted Miss Havisham is also Magwitch's old partner in crime and hated enemy.
Characters in Great Expectations.Oliver Twist: Dickens's famous orphan who asks for more belongs to another novel, published in 1838, about twenty years before Great Expectations.
Characters in Great Expectations.Fagin: The sinister leader of the child pickpockets is from Oliver Twist; no such gang appears in Pip's story.
Characters in Great Expectations.Artful Dodger: Jack Dawkins, the cheeky young pickpocket, lives in Oliver Twist; Pip's world has no such lovable thief.
Characters in Great Expectations.Bill Sikes: The brutal burglar who murders Nancy and his dog Bull's-eye belong to Oliver Twist, not Great Expectations.
Characters in Great Expectations.Nancy: The tragic thief who tries to protect Oliver is from Oliver Twist, and her murder was among Dickens's most shocking scenes.
Characters in Great Expectations.Ebenezer Scrooge: The miser who learns generosity on Christmas Eve belongs to A Christmas Carol (1843), another Dickens book.
Characters in Great Expectations.Tiny Tim: The frail son of Bob Cratchit, who says "God bless us, every one", is from A Christmas Carol, not Great Expectations.
Characters in Great Expectations.Bob Cratchit: Scrooge's underpaid clerk is a Christmas Carol figure; Great Expectations has Wemmick as its clerk instead.
Characters in Great Expectations.Uriah Heep: The creepily "humble" clerk who keeps wringing his hands is from David Copperfield, a different Dickens novel.
Characters in Great Expectations.Mr. Micawber: The perpetually broke optimist who is always waiting for "something to turn up" is from David Copperfield.
Characters in Great Expectations.David Copperfield: Dickens called this his "favourite child" among his novels; it's a different hero with a different story from Pip's.
Characters in Great Expectations.Little Nell: The doomed child of The Old Curiosity Shop was so beloved that readers famously begged Dickens to spare her; he didn't.

Characters in Animal Farm.Napoleon: Napoleon is the boar who seizes control of the farm, standing in for Stalin in Orwell's allegory.
Characters in Animal Farm.Snowball: Snowball is the pig who is driven out, based on Trotsky, and who draws up plans for a windmill.
Characters in Animal Farm.Boxer: Boxer is the loyal cart-horse whose mottos are I will work harder and Napoleon is always right; he's sent to the knacker.
Characters in Animal Farm.Clover: Clover is a motherly mare who senses the farm has betrayed its ideals, but can't put it into words.
Characters in Animal Farm.Benjamin: Benjamin is the cynical donkey who can read as well as any pig, but he refuses to get involved until it's too late.
Characters in Animal Farm.Mollie: Mollie is a vain mare who loves ribbons and sugar, and who leaves the farm for a human life.
Characters in Animal Farm.Moses: Moses is the tame raven who spreads tales of Sugarcandy Mountain, representing religion in the allegory.
Characters in Animal Farm.Squealer: Squealer is the pig whose persuasive speech rewrites the Commandments, as Orwell's propaganda minister.
Characters in Animal Farm.Old Major: Old Major is the prize boar whose dream sets off the rebellion, and his skull is displayed afterward, like Lenin's body.
Characters in Animal Farm.Muriel: Muriel is the wise white goat who reads the Commandments for the others, and who notices the changes.
Characters in Animal Farm.Mr. Jones: Mr. Jones is the drunken farmer of Manor Farm, driven out when the animals rise up.
Characters in Animal Farm.Mr. Pilkington: Mr. Pilkington owns Foxwood, a shabby farm, and represents the British, according to readers of the allegory.
Characters in Animal Farm.Mr. Frederick: Mr. Frederick owns Pinchfield and is a hard man who tricks the animals with forged banknotes, standing for Germany.
Characters in Animal Farm.Winston Smith: Winston Smith is the hero of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, not Animal Farm, though both are by Orwell.
Characters in Animal Farm.Big Brother: Big Brother is the Party's watchful leader in Nineteen Eighty-Four, and his poster says he's watching you.
Characters in Animal Farm.Julia: Julia is Winston's lover in Nineteen Eighty-Four, a rebel in secret in a world of strict control.
Characters in Animal Farm.O'Brien: O'Brien is the Inner Party official who tortures Winston in Nineteen Eighty-Four.
Characters in Animal Farm.Emmanuel Goldstein: Emmanuel Goldstein is the Party's supposed arch-enemy in Nineteen Eighty-Four, loathed in the Two Minutes Hate.
Characters in Animal Farm.Wilbur: Wilbur is the pig in E. B. White's Charlotte's Web, saved from slaughter by a spider's words.
Characters in Animal Farm.Charlotte: Charlotte is the spider in Charlotte's Web who weaves words like Some Pig into her web to save Wilbur.
Characters in Animal Farm.Templeton: Templeton is the greedy rat in Charlotte's Web who helps Charlotte, but only for food.
Characters in Animal Farm.Babe: Babe is the sheep-herding pig from Dick King-Smith's The Sheep-Pig, not an Orwell creation.
Characters in Animal Farm.Black Beauty: Black Beauty is the horse narrator of Anna Sewell's 1877 novel, not part of Orwell's farm.
Characters in Animal Farm.Hazel: Hazel is the rabbit leader in Richard Adams's Watership Down, an animal tale of a different kind.

Epic poems.The Iliad: The Iliad takes place over only a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War, focusing on Achilles' rage.
Epic poems.The Odyssey: The Odyssey follows Odysseus's ten-year journey home and was traditionally recited by bards.
Epic poems.The Aeneid: The Aeneid is Virgil's Latin epic about Trojan Aeneas; Virgil reportedly asked that it be burned on his deathbed.
Epic poems.Beowulf: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, which was damaged in a 1731 library fire.
Epic poems.Paradise Lost: Paradise Lost is John Milton's 1667 epic about Satan's fall, which he dictated after going blind.
Epic poems.The Divine Comedy: The Divine Comedy is Dante's journey through hell, purgatory, and paradise, written in Italian, not Latin.
Epic poems.Gilgamesh: Gilgamesh is one of the oldest known literary works, written on clay tablets in ancient Mesopotamia.
Epic poems.Mahabharata: The Mahabharata is the longest epic ever, many times longer than the Iliad and Odyssey combined.
Epic poems.Ramayana: The Ramayana is the Sanskrit epic of Prince Rama's quest to rescue his wife Sita from the demon king Ravana.
Epic poems.The Faerie Queene: The Faerie Queene is Edmund Spenser's unfinished allegorical epic, which flatters Queen Elizabeth I.
Epic poems.Song of Roland: The Song of Roland is among the oldest major works of French literature, recounting a heroic last stand.
Epic poems.Kalevala: The Kalevala is Finland's national epic, compiled by Elias Lönnrot, and a key influence on Tolkien.
Epic poems.Nibelungenlied: The Nibelungenlied is a medieval German epic of Siegfried, which Wagner turned into his Ring cycle.
Epic poems.Hamlet: Hamlet is Shakespeare's tragedy about a Danish prince, a play and not an epic poem.
Epic poems.Don Quixote: Don Quixote is Cervantes's novel of 1605, often called the first modern novel, not an epic poem.
Epic poems.War and Peace: War and Peace is Tolstoy's enormous novel, epic in scope but written in prose, so not an epic poem.
Epic poems.Moby-Dick: Moby-Dick is Melville's novel, with epic ambitions, but it's prose, not a poem.
Epic poems.Ulysses: Ulysses is Joyce's novel, which follows a single day in Dublin and echoes the Odyssey, but it's prose.
Epic poems.The Raven: The Raven is Poe's famous poem, but at 108 lines, it's a short narrative rather than an epic.
Epic poems.Ozymandias: Ozymandias is Shelley's 14-line sonnet about a ruined statue, far too brief to be an epic.
Epic poems.The Waste Land: The Waste Land is T. S. Eliot's long, fragmentary modernist poem, but it's not a traditional epic.
Epic poems.Oedipus Rex: Oedipus Rex is a Greek tragedy by Sophocles, a play rather than an epic poem.
Epic poems.Gulliver's Travels: Gulliver's Travels is Swift's satirical prose, and it's a novel-like satire, not an epic poem.
Epic poems.Les Misérables: Les Misérables is Victor Hugo's sprawling novel, which is epic in scope but not a poem.

Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Harlequin: A witty, acrobatic servant in a diamond costume, whose slapstick bat gave English the word "slapstick".
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Pierrot: A sad, white-faced fool, adapted in French pantomime from the Italian Pedrolino, and a favorite of Parisian Romantics.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Columbine: A clever maid and Harlequin's lover, her name from the Italian Colombina, meaning "little dove".
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Pantalone: A greedy old Venetian merchant whose long trousers, "pantaloons", are the source of the English word "pants".
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Il Dottore: A pompous Bolognese scholar who spouts fake Latin and has little real knowledge, a pedant who's always wrong.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Scaramouche: A cowardly braggart dressed in black, his name comes from "skirmish", and Sabatini's 1921 novel borrowed it.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Pulcinella: A hook-nosed Neapolitan trickster in a white costume, and the ancestor of Punch in Punch and Judy.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Brighella: A scheming servant from Bergamo, in green and white, who is always ready to cheat and flatter.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Il Capitano: A boastful soldier who turns out to be a coward, a stock mask of the Italian stage who brags about imaginary conquests.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Zanni: The servant characters of commedia, and the origin of the English word "zany", for a clownish person.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Figaro: Beaumarchais's clever barber is a descendant of commedia servants, but a full character, not a stock type.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Don Giovanni: Mozart's 1787 opera about the Don Juan legend, whose hero is a distinct person and not a commedia mask.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Falstaff: Shakespeare's fat knight resembles Il Capitano, but he is an original creation, not a stock mask.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Cyrano: The real Cyrano de Bergerac inspired Rostand's 1897 play, a swordsman and poet, not a stock character.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Tartuffe: Molière's hypocrite, in a play banned for five years. Molière took inspiration from commedia, but Tartuffe is an individual.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Faust: Goethe's scholar who sells his soul to the devil is a tragic individual, not a stock type from commedia.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Mephistopheles: The devil in Faust is a distinct creation of German legend and not one of commedia's masks.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Hamlet: A Danish prince and an original tragic hero, though he too hides behind an "antic disposition".
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Cinderella: Hardly. The rags-to-riches girl of Perrault's fairy tale is no commedia mask, nor an official stock type.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Pinocchio: Collodi's wooden puppet of 1883, who has a long nose, is a fairy-tale hero, not a commedia mask.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Puck: Shakespeare's sprite from A Midsummer Night's Dream is a fairy-folk figure, not a commedia stock role.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie's boy who wouldn't grow up, from a 1904 play, is an original character, not a mask.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Willy Loman: Arthur Miller's 1949 salesman is a realistic modern character, not a stock one from old Italian farce.
Commedia dell'arte stock characters.Romeo: Shakespeare's lover from Verona is Italian but not a mask, and he's an original tragic hero.
